lead: This unit explains how operating systems store data permanently and move it between memory and devices. After finishing, the student can describe file structures, choose allocation methods, and evaluate I/O performance.
about: Unit 5 contains nine chapters that start with the basic idea of a file, its attributes and ways to read or write it (5.1). It then shows how files are organized in directories (5.2) and how external file systems are attached and shared (5.3). The internal layout of a file system and the virtual file system layer follow (5.4). Allocation strategies for placing file blocks are covered next (5.5) and the techniques for tracking free space (5.6). Chapters 5.7 and 5.8 move to the hardware mechanisms for I/O and the software stack that buffers and caches data. The final chapter (5.9) studies the physical disk layout and the algorithms that order requests to minimise seek time.

chapters.idea: Define a file, its attributes and the two main access methods.
chapters.depth: Explain file as a named collection of bytes. List attributes: name, type, size, timestamps, permissions. Describe sequential (read/write in order) and direct/random access. Some syllabi call this "File System Interface" or "File Concept".

figure.title: File request flow
figure.aria: Shows the flow from an application request to the storage device.

chapters.example: A program creates a file of 0 KB, writes 120 bytes, then reads 50 bytes sequentially. What is the final file size? Answer: 120 bytes.
chapters.trap: Confusing sequential access with the file being stored sequentially on disk.

chapters.idea: Show how directories organise files in a hierarchy.
chapters.depth: Describe flat and hierarchical directories. Explain directory entry (name + inode). Discuss path resolution and absolute vs relative paths. Some syllabi refer to this as "Directory Structure".
chapters.example: Given the path /home/raju/docs/report.txt, list the inode numbers: / (2), home (5), raju (9), docs (12), report.txt (15).
chapters.trap: Treating a directory entry as the actual file data.
chapters.leave: Mounting and sharing of file systems.

chapters.idea: Explain mounting a file system and basic file sharing.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this. Briefly define mount point, mount system call, virtual file system (VFS) role, and an example of NFS sharing. Mention that mounting does not copy data.

figure.title: Mount integration
figure.aria: Mount integrates a file system into the VFS and can expose remote shares.

chapters.example: Mount a 4 GB USB drive at /media/usb. After copying a 200 MB video, how much free space remains? Answer: 3.8 GB.
chapters.trap: Assuming mount copies the whole file system to the local disk.
chapters.leave: Detailed VFS design and file-system internal structures.

chapters.idea: Describe the internal layout of a file system and the VFS abstraction.
chapters.depth: Cover superblock, inode table, data blocks, free‑block bitmap. Explain how VFS maps generic calls to specific FS operations. Some syllabi label this "File System Structure".

figure.title: FS internal components
figure.aria: Internal components of a typical UNIX‑like file system.

chapters.example: A disk has 1024 blocks. Block 0 holds the superblock, block 1‑4 hold the inode table, and block 5 holds the free bitmap. If inode 7 points to blocks 20‑22, what are the physical block numbers of the file? Answer: 20, 21, 22.
chapters.trap: Mixing up inode numbers with data‑block numbers.

chapters.idea: Compare contiguous, linked and indexed allocation of file blocks.
chapters.depth: Explain each method, show how pointers are stored, discuss fragmentation and overhead. Some syllabi call this "Allocation Methods".
chapters.example: A file of 5 KB (5 blocks) is stored contiguously starting at block 20, linked with pointers starting at block 30, and indexed with a single‑level index block 40. List the block numbers used in each method.
chapters.trap: Assuming indexed allocation always needs one extra block per file regardless of size.

chapters.idea: Show how the OS tracks free blocks on a disk.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this. Summarise bit‑vector, free‑block linked list and grouping. Explain how allocation and deallocation update the map.
chapters.example: A 16‑block disk has the bit vector 1100 0111 1111 0000. Which is the first free block? Answer: block 2.
chapters.trap: Forgetting to clear the bit after freeing a block.

chapters.idea: Describe polling, interrupts and DMA as hardware I/O mechanisms.
chapters.depth: Define polling loop, interrupt request, interrupt service routine and DMA controller. Compare latency and CPU utilisation.
chapters.example: Transferring 4 KB via DMA takes 2 ms. The same transfer by polling needs 8 ms. What is the speed‑up factor? Answer: 4× faster.
chapters.trap: Mixing up interrupt latency with the time taken by DMA to move data.

chapters.idea: Explain the OS I/O software stack, drivers, buffering and caching.
chapters.depth: Show layers: application → OS API → device driver → buffer cache → hardware. Define write‑through vs write‑back, read‑ahead and page cache. Some syllabi label this "I/O Software".

figure.title: I/O software layers
figure.aria: Software layers from application to hardware with buffering.

chapters.example: Reading an 8 KB file with a 4 KB buffer requires how many device reads? Answer: 2 reads.
chapters.trap: Assuming a cache eliminates all disk accesses for a newly opened file.

chapters.idea: Present disk geometry and scheduling algorithms to reduce seek time.
chapters.depth: Cover tracks, cylinders, seek time, rotational latency. Explain FCFS, SSTF, SCAN, C‑SCAN, LOOK. Provide formula for average seek = total movement ÷ number of requests.

figure.aria: Head movement graph for the request sequence used in FCFS.

chapters.example: Requests: 55, 58, 39, 18, 90. Head starts at 50. Compute total head movement for FCFS (5+3+19+21+72 = 120 cylinders) and for SCAN (moving outward then inward gives 92 cylinders).
chapters.trap: Forgetting to include the distance from the initial head position to the first request.
